# **Closing the door behind: metric‑based research evaluation ** **systems and gatekeeping towards young researchers**
**Hakan Soner Şener1** ** · İdris Semih Kaya2** ** · Mücella Sena Köksal2** ** · Zehra Taşkın2,****[3](http://orcid.org/0000-0001-7102-493X)**
Received: 28 August 2024 / Accepted: 4 March 2025 / Published online: 28 March 2025 © The Author(s) 2025
#### **Abstract**
The competitive nature of academia has led to the establishment of rigorous criteria by decision-makers for evaluating researchers' performances. Title and tenure systems have been implemented based on these specifc criteria. This study aims to examine how these criteria are fulflled, identify which groups of researchers are required to meet these performance indicators, and assess the extent to which they do so. Data were collected from 98 academics in the feld of library and information science via the Web of Science and the main academic platform of the Council of Higher Education, Turkey. A total of 1641 articles and 999 books or book chapters were subjected to analysis. The fndings suggest that early-career researchers are disproportionately compelled to adhere to the "publish or perish" paradigm and are expected to meet higher performance expectations. When normalized for years of experience, the results indicate that professors exhibit the lowest publication output, while faculty members with a Ph.D. who hold the title of Associate Professor demonstrate the highest output. While this study primarily focuses on comparing the fulfllment of criteria between decision-makers and early-career researchers, future research will explore the observed infation in book and book chapter publications within the same feld.
**Keywords** Title system · Academic performance evaluation · Academic career · Gatekeeping · Higher education · Turkey
## **Introduction**
In the competitive and demanding world of academia, early-career researchers often face the daunting challenge of navigating the "publish or perish" paradigm. To successfully publish their research in academic journals, these researchers are expected to meet specifc criteria (Gardner, [2008;](#page-17-0) Janger & Nowotny, [2013;](#page-18-0) Mantai, [2017;](#page-18-1) Stewart & Kirkbride,

However, these criteria are constantly evolving, introducing new barriers to career advancement (Austin & Rice, [1998](#page-17-1); Laudel, [2017;](#page-18-2) Miller, [2022](#page-18-3)). Consequently, the issue of gatekeeping in academic careers has become increasingly concerning and warrants critical examination (Nästesjö, [2021;](#page-18-4) Önder & Erdil,[ 2015](#page-18-5); Tütüncü, [2023,](#page-19-1)[ 2024](#page-19-2)).
The primary objective of this study is to assess whether decision-makers adhere to the research evaluation criteria expected of early-career researchers. Our focus is on the associate professor title system employed by the Interuniversity Board of the Higher Education Council in Turkey. Specifcally, the study addresses the following research questions:
- To what extent do decision-makers (panel evaluators) in the higher education system meet the criteria expected of early-career researchers? - Which type of criterion is most frequently fulflled? - When comparing early-career researchers with decision-makers, which group demonstrates a higher rate of criterion fulflment?
An important aspect of research evaluation systems lies in their epistemological underpinnings, particularly regarding what constitutes a "proper" measurement in education (Hefernan, [2021)](#page-18-6). The reliance on publication counts, citation metrics, and journal impact factors refects certain assumptions about academic productivity and quality that may not fully capture the breadth of scholarly contributions, especially in diverse felds such as library and information science. A critical examination of these epistemological issues is essential to understand the broader implications of such metrics for academic evaluation systems globally (Huang et al.,[ 2022](#page-18-7)).
While this study focuses on the evolving associate professorship system in Turkey, similar patterns of metric-based evaluation and its unintended consequences are evident in other cultures and regions, such as Europe and Latin America (Krawczyk & Kulczycki, [2021;](#page-18-8) Vessuri et al., [2014)](#page-19-3). In these contexts, the increasing emphasis on quantitative metrics to evaluate academic performance has similarly led to challenges, including the prioritization of high-impact journals, the proliferation of questionable publishing practices, and heightened pressures on early-career researchers. By acknowledging these parallels, this study aims to situate its fndings within a broader global context, enhancing its relevance for international scholars.
An examination of Turkey's associate professorship system ofers a historical perspective that facilitates comprehension of the present situation. As time has passed, the criteria for obtaining this title have placed increasing emphasis on publications as a primary measure of academic merit. This shift can be attributed to the evolution of higher education policies and priorities. The 2024 revisions to the criteria, which were implemented with the objective of enhancing research standards and productivity, have brought to light the unintended consequences of metric-based systems. These unintended consequences include pressures to publish in questionable venues. These reforms underscore the systemic challenges confronting early-career researchers (Bülbül,[ 2021](#page-17-2)), thereby connecting the empirical fndings of this study to broader theoretical discourses on gatekeeping and academic evaluation.
#### **Gatekeeping in academia**
Gatekeeping, a well-established concept in the social sciences, refers to individuals or groups with the authority to control access to resources or positions (Cook & Fonow, [1984;](#page-17-3)
[FIGURE: see LR.R37_fig02.jpg]
Husu & de Cheveigné, [2010)](#page-18-9). In academia, gatekeeping occurs through both internal and external mechanisms, infuencing everything from hiring and promotion to funding and publishing (Forsberg et al., [2022](#page-17-4)). This study focuses on ongoing academic gatekeeping, particularly in the context of panel evaluation processes.
The implications of gatekeeping extend beyond individual researchers, shaping systemic issues within academia. The pressure to meet rigid evaluation criteria has exacerbated job insecurity and led to the casualization of academic labor, particularly for early-career researchers. This environment, driven by metrics and competition, often intensifes stress and mental health challenges among scholars. Furthermore, current practices that prioritize quantity over quality and established networks over emerging voices risk stifing innovation and reducing diversity in research (McFadyen & Rankin,[ 2016](#page-18-10)).
To understand the persistence of these gatekeeping mechanisms, it is crucial to examine their historical and systemic roots. The emergence of precarious academic working conditions and the growing reliance on metrics are closely tied to the rise of neoliberal policies (Zhang & Gong, [2024)](#page-19-4). Neoliberalism, which gained prominence in the 1980s under leaders like Reagan and Thatcher, introduced external actors—politicians, policymakers, and decision-makers—into academia, shaping its outputs and defning "quality" in academic work (Mula-Falcón & Caballero,[ 2022](#page-18-11); Rosa, [2010)](#page-18-12).
University ranking systems, citation metrics, and performance indicators have become hallmarks of the neoliberal academic system, infuencing career trajectories and institutional success (Westerheijden, [2022](#page-19-5)). Scholars now feel compelled to relentlessly pursue publications as a measure of success, raising questions about the long-term value of these criteria and their potential evolution (Lee, [2014;](#page-18-13) Posselt,[ 2016](#page-18-14); Rosa, [2020)](#page-18-15).
Beyond neoliberalism, managerialism and bureaucratic rationalization have further entrenched metric-based governance in academia. These frameworks emphasize operational efciency, accountability, and performance measurement, often embedding quantitative evaluations to justify funding decisions. While these practices aim to enhance governance, they frequently align with external socio-economic pressures, including global competition among universities and national strategies prioritizing international rankings (Dutta et al., [2022;](#page-17-5) Hammarfelt & Hallonsten,[ 2022](#page-18-16); Zhang,[ 2024](#page-19-6)). These dynamics underscore the complexity of gatekeeping, refecting not only market-oriented priorities but also broader systemic forces in higher education (Fanelli, [2010](#page-17-6); Marginson & van der Wende, [2007)](#page-18-17).
Internal gatekeeping within academia is equally signifcant, involving a range of actors such as research councils, panels, editors, reviewers, and senior faculty members (Husu & de Cheveigné, [2010;](#page-18-9) Montgomery, [2020)](#page-18-18). This process is especially prominent in higher education admissions, hiring, tenure, and promotion decisions. Modern academic expectations for productivity surpass those of previous generations, creating precarious conditions for early-career researchers (Austin & Rice, [1998](#page-17-1); Bieber, [1997;](#page-17-7) Massy & Wilger, [1995;](#page-18-19) Sorcinelli,[ 1994](#page-18-20)).
Gatekeeping also manifests across various domains of academic life, including publications, funding, employment, ideas, and social networks (Cook & Fonow, [1984](#page-17-3)). These networks—formal and informal—play a pivotal role in shaping access to opportunities like collaborations, funding, and publication venues (Hefernan, [2021;](#page-18-6) Mishra, [2020](#page-18-21)). Earlycareer researchers, often lacking established connections, are disproportionately disadvantaged, which perpetuates existing inequalities and limits diverse perspectives in academic discourse (McFadyen & Rankin, [2016)](#page-18-10).
Furthermore, the actions of journal editors, reviewers, and policymakers are central to academic gatekeeping but are often fraught with unintended consequences. For example,
[FIGURE: see LR.R37_fig03.jpg]
journal editors and reviewers may favor articles published in high-impact journals, sidelining innovative research from emerging or interdisciplinary felds (Taşkın et al., [2022](#page-19-7)). Similarly, policymakers who enforce rigid promotion criteria may inadvertently incentivize practices such as publishing in questionable journals to meet quantitative targets (Öztürk & Taşkın,[ 2024](#page-18-22)).
An illustrative example of gatekeeping's evolving nature is the associate professorship system in Turkey. The Interuniversity Board of the Higher Education Council periodically revises criteria for achieving this rank to uphold academic standards. However, these frequent changes can create uncertainty and additional challenges for academics, refecting the dynamic and often unpredictable nature of gatekeeping in academia.
Gatekeeping mechanisms—spanning publication requirements, funding allocations, and employment opportunities—shape academic careers, particularly for early-career researchers. Understanding these dynamics and addressing their systemic roots is essential for fostering a more equitable and innovative academic environment.
## **Ever‑shifting landscape of Turkey's associate professor title system**
Turkey's associate professorship system is a two-stage process. In the frst stage, the title of associate professor is conferred by the Council of Higher Education. Once this title is obtained, candidates can apply for associate professor positions at individual universities (Öztürk & Taşkın, [2024](#page-18-22)). While the criteria for obtaining the title are standardized across Turkey, the criteria for specifc positions are determined by the universities ofering them. Since the title criteria are uniform nationwide, the path to achieving associate professorship title in Turkey has been shaped by a series of reforms and adaptations over time.
The associate professorship system in Turkey dates back to 1934, with its inception in the Instructions of Istanbul University. Since then, the landscape has continuously evolved (Baltacı, [2022](#page-17-8); Demirbilek & Çetin, [2022)](#page-17-9). Various criteria—such as foreign language profciency, teaching experience, oral interviews, a requisite number of publications, and panel evaluations—have been integrated into the system. Prior to the establishment of the Higher Education Council in 1981, changes focused on criteria like test lectures, age limits, experience, and foreign language profciency. However, following the Council's establishment, the most signifcant changes centered on the number of publications and panel evaluations (Demirbilek & Çetin, [2022](#page-17-9)). Since the 2000s, the number of publications has become the most important—and sometimes the sole—criterion for associate professorship title appointments.
One of the most signifcant changes occurred in 2024, when the criteria points were radically altered, sparking widespread debate within Turkey's academic community[.1](#page-3-0) The rationale behind these revisions has been twofold: to enhance the number of scientifc research and to elevate the standards expected of those conferred with the title of associate professor. However, against the backdrop of a burgeoning academic landscape, heightened competition, and the pervasive infuence of publishing conglomerates, evaluating the scholarly credentials of researchers has become increasingly complex. Consequently, numerical metrics have gained prominence, fostering a culture of rapid and expedited publishing
(Tonta, [2017)](#page-19-8). Alarmingly, studies have indicated that these promotion and appointment systems have inadvertently incentivized researchers in Turkey to publish in questionable journals (Öztürk & Taşkın, [2024)](#page-18-22).
This phenomenon has ensnared early-career researchers in a relentless cycle of "publish or perish," from the completion of their doctoral studies to the application for associate professorship, inadvertently perpetuating the neoliberal ethos within academia. As they navigate these challenges, the pursuit of academic excellence becomes intertwined with the exigencies of survival in an increasingly competitive scholarly environment.
# **Data and methods**
#### **Data collection**
To address the research questions of this study, we selected the feld of library and information science, a domain where scientometrics and research evaluation studies are also conducted. Until the mid-1950s, this feld in Turkey was largely based on a master-apprentice model, with training provided through courses. Formal university education in this feld began with the establishment of the Librarianship Institute at Ankara University in 1954 (Atılgan, [1995](#page-17-10)). Over the years, the department has evolved to include specializations such as librarianship, archival studies, and documentation/information. Today, it is consolidated under the name "Department of Information and Records Management." As of 2024, the feld ofers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral programs at 14 universities, including 13 state universities and one foundation university, with a total of 275 academic staf[.2](#page-4-0)
The 98 academics included in this study were selected based on their afliation with state universities ofering programs in library and information science in Turkey. The selection criteria focused on academics holding titles such as professor, associate professor, and faculty members with Ph.D.s, while excluding research assistants and lecturers, as they are not required to publish under the associate professorship evaluation system. Detailed information about 98 academics was collected from the main academic platform/database of the Council of Higher Education.[3](#page-4-1) The platform of the Council of Higher Education is an ofcial database listing all academics working in Turkey. All academics in the higher education system are recorded in this database by the Council. Applications for the title of associate professor and the publication-based academic incentive allowance system for academics at state universities are processed through records entered by academics in this database. Thus, the database is crucial as it provides access to the publications of all academics working in Turkey, along with their declarations in promotion and incentive fles. Information about the academic careers of 98 academics, their publications, and the theses they supervised was obtained from this database. Additionally, the Web of Science profles of these academics were accessed through individual queries conducted in March 2024.
After collecting all publications and other relevant information, a thorough data cleaning and standardization process was conducted. Non-refereed publications and works published in 2024 were excluded from the study as these entries could introduce variability unrelated to the established criteria for academic evaluation. For journal quartile information, we used the quartiles of the latest available year, as journal ranking systems undergo periodic changes, and some journals may no longer be indexed. If a journal was no longer indexed, the last available quartile was used. This approach was necessary due to data availability issues, as impact factors are not consistently accessible for all years, particularly for journals that have ceased indexing. Additionally, using a uniform time frame ensured comparability across all journals, avoiding inconsistencies that arise from fluctuating rankings. It is important to note that quartile information was used solely in the Article Criteria Fulfillment Scores by Titles section for point calculations, which had minimal impact on our overall findings. As emphasized throughout the paper, our primary focus is on the inequalities inherent in point-based systems, and we did not use Journal Impact Factor (JIF) or quartile rankings as a direct analytical component of our study.
### **Analysis **
In this study, we calculated the point scores of academics based on relevant policies and then implemented statistical tests to determine significant differences. The Kruskal–Wallis test and the Mann–Whitney U test were employed to analyze the data and identify statistically significant differences between the groups. Additionally, effect sizes were calculated to quantify the magnitude of these differences, using the formulas provided by Cohen (2013).

$$ Mann Whitney Ur_G = 2(\overline{R}_A - \overline{R}_B)/N_T (2) $$
For data visualization, we utilized various tools. Sankey diagrams were created using Flourish Studio<sup>4</sup> to illustrate the flow and relationships within the data. Violin plots were generated using the R Commander kmggplot<sup>5</sup> plugin to display the distribution of point scores across different academic ranks. Scatterplots were produced in Excel to examine correlations and trends within the data. All statistical tests were conducted using IBM SPSS 23, ensuring robust and reliable analysis. The combination of these tools and statistical methods allowed for a comprehensive examination of the point scores and the identification of key patterns and differences among the academic groups.
The study employed diverse data visualization methods, including Sankey diagrams, violin plots, and scatterplots, to enhance the interpretability of the findings. Sankey diagrams effectively illustrate the flow and relationships within the data, making complex interactions between variables more accessible. Violin plots were chosen for their ability to display the distribution and density of point scores across different academic ranks, while

Despite the rigor of the methodology, certain limitations warrant acknowledgment. The reliance on data extracted from a single academic database, while comprehensive, may not encompass all relevant academic outputs. Additionally, self-reported publication data could introduce biases; however, the rigorous data cleaning and verifcation processes employed aimed to minimize such risks.
## **Findings**
#### **Web of science profles of information science academics**
Web of Science is the essential research evaluation tool in Turkey and most points are given to Web of Science publications in almost all research evaluation systems. According to the latest changes in the associate professorship title criteria, a researcher has to collect 10 points from Web of Science publications as an obligatory rule, also the criteria points are determined by using Web of Science quartiles. For example, an article indexed in Web of Science Q1 is worth 30 points, while an ESCI-indexed publication is worth 10 points (The Council of Higher Education, Turkey, [2024)](#page-19-9).
Figure [1](#page-6-0) shows Web of Science profles of researchers working in library and information science in Turkey. The analysis indicates that early-career researchers face disadvantages in terms of publication and citation metrics, particularly when compared to more established academics. While this fnding aligns with existing literature on the challenges faced by early-career researchers, it is important to acknowledge that these observations are based on quantitative data and may not fully capture the nuances of individual career trajectories. As the literature already mentioned, the h-index is not an efective tool for

evaluating researchers' careers, especially for early-career researchers (de Rijcke et al., 2021). However, having a 5 h-index indicates 5 points in the associate professorship title system (The Council of Higher Education, Turkey, 2024). Figure 1a shows that only 9 people meet that criterion (10%). Four of them are professors, two are associate professors, and three are faculty members with Ph.D. with associate professor titles. Six of these academics work for the same institution. All these findings indicate that the h-index is not an accurate tool to evaluate the library and information science field, while publication and citation density is low. On the other hand, some senior scholars achieve high h-index scores, which may be influenced by their established reputations and networks within their fields or sub-disciplines. However, it is essential to recognize that the h-index does not exclusively reflect research impact but may also be shaped by factors such as career duration and disciplinary norms. These inequalities were confirmed by statistical test results. According to Kruskal Wallis test, there is a significant difference between the h-index and titles (H(3) = 18.499, p < 0.001, \eta^{\rm H}_2 = 0.144). While there is no significant difference between professors and associate professors, when four groups are compared in pairs using the Mann Whitney U test, the results for comparisons covering faculty members with Ph.D. were statistically significant.6
Although the number of publications by professors seems high in Fig. 1b, and it is statistically significant (H(3) = 14.968, p = 0.002, \eta_2^H = 0.106), when it is normalized using experience years, there is no difference by title (p = 0.556). The lowest Web of Science publication output is identified for professors (average = 0.34, median = 0.24), followed by Associate Professors (average = 0.66, median = 0.25), Faculty members with Ph.D. (average = 0.69, median = 0.33) and Faculty members with Ph.D. with Associate Professor title (average = 0.73, median = 0.66).
Citations are an important part of the associate professorship system of Turkey, especially citations from the Web of Science. While a citation in Web of Science equals 3 points, it is 1 or 2 for other sources. While the average number of citations per Professor is 1.55 (median=0.32), it is 1.42 for Faculty members with Ph.D. (median=0.8), 10.3 for Faculty members with Ph.D. with Associate Professor title (median=1.46), and 4.44 for associate professors (median=1.06). These scores are expected for faculty members with Ph.D. since they have short experience in the field and do not have sufficient time to get enough citations, however, it is an interesting result for professors while they will be the panel evaluators of these early-career researchers.

#### Differences on author declarations: conceptualisation problem
Before investigating the distribution of articles based on titles, it's crucial to highlight a significant aspect of the associate professorship title system in Turkey: the weighting of international publications. As the term "international" lacks a precise definition, allowing authors to categorize articles published in Turkey-addressed and Turkish language journals as international. This phenomenon stems from the criteria, which prioritize a journal's

inclusion in international indexes over factors like language, thematic focus, or publisher location.
Figure[ 2](#page-8-0) illustrate authors' statements regarding their articles. These declarations reveal that authors earn points by designating their Turkish-language articles, published by local or regional publishers, as international. Conversely, despite being published in English or by international publishing houses, some articles are labeled as national due to the system's requirement for a minimum of three national publications. This practice persists even when such articles yield low scores, underscoring a conceptual defcit within the system.
#### **Huge increase in the number of articles after 2015**
There are two major journals in the feld of library and information science in Turkey: *Turkish Librarianship (Türk Kütüphaneciliği—since 1952)*[7](#page-8-1) and *Information World (Bilgi * *Dünyası—since 2000)*. [8](#page-8-2) Both journals are published by associations—the Turkish Librarians' Association and the University and Research Librarians' Association, respectively. These journals accounted for 38% of the works published in the feld up until 2023, highlighting their signifcant role.
However, since 2015, there has been a notable increase in the number of articles published by university journals, which has even surpassed the publications from associations over the past fve years. Additionally, 2015 saw the emergence of individually run local journals. One of the main reasons for this shift is likely the academic incentive allowance regulation started to be implemented in 2015 which aims to grant academics at state universities annual salary bonuses based on the number of publications they produce (Akademik Teşvik Ödeneği Yönetmeliği [Academic Incentive Allowance Code], [2020)](#page-17-13).[9](#page-8-3) As a result, the landscape of library and information science in Turkey, which had remained

The total number of Q1 publications in the feld of library and information science is 24 (1.5%). The possibility of getting the highest score is hard to achieve for most of the scholars working in the feld. Additionally, the requirement for national articles increased from three in 2023 to fve in 2024, with three of these fve publications needing to be single-authored. Since these changes are in line with the publishing practices of the feld of library and information science, which is a small branch of social sciences, it is inevitable that there are no signifcant diferences in scores between the criteria. However, important diferences are found for books and book chapters published in the feld.
## **Books and book chapters**
### **Book infation in library and information science**
As shown in Fig.[ 5,](#page-11-0) there has been a remarkable increase in the number of books and book chapters published, especially since 2015. This surge can be attributed to the academic incentive allowance regulation introduced in 2015, similar to the one for articles. The
[FIGURE: see LR.R37_fig11.jpg]
**Fig.** **5 **Number of books/book chapters in library and information science feld by publisher type and year
[FIGURE: see LR.R37_fig12.jpg]
impact of the 2015 change is evident in the rise in published books and book chapters. Figure [5 ](#page-11-0)illustrates that 999 books or book chapters were published between 1980 and 2023, based on data collected from academics' declarations. Of these, 710 publications (71%) were published after 2015.
A similar conceptualization problem defned for articles' audiences (national/international) is observed with books and book chapters. Until 2023, the criteria required that a book publishing house must have been operating for at least four years to be recognized. A national publishing house must be cataloged in university libraries in Turkey, while an international publishing house must be cataloged in the library of a university ranked among the top 500 by any ranking organization. This can be seen as a practice related to LibCitation. However, the main purpose of LibCitation is to reveal the cultural impact of books and determine the bestsellers in libraries. It is concerned with how many diferent libraries catalog a book, not whether a book is cataloged in a single library (White et al., [2009)](#page-19-10). Furthermore, this measure does not refect the quality of the book but rather the prestige of the publisher and the popularity of the book. Additionally, factors such as libraries' cataloging policies, donation policies, and reader demands may afect a book's availability in libraries.
Recognizing these issues, the Higher Education Council revised the criteria and adopted the Book Citation Index (BKCI) as a "quality" scale for books. Books indexed in BKCI now receive 20 points, and book chapters receive 10 points, while other books and book chapters receive 5 and 3 points, respectively. However, as of September 2023, only three books from Turkey are indexed in BKCI, along with 10,494 book chapters (Taşkın, [2023](#page-19-11)), and the criteria does not ft the publication practices of Turkey, especially for SSH felds.
The new system also requires a minimum of two books or book chapters. Due to the infationary efects of previous policies, a maximum limit of 20 points for all books and 5 points for locally published books was introduced in the 2024 update. It is too early to monitor the efects of the current scoring system on book publishing, but future studies are needed to understand the efects of metric and index-based research evaluation systems on scientifc felds.

However, it should be noted that a declaration from the publisher stating that the publishing house is international is sufcient to classify Turkish-language and Turkey-based publishers as international publishers. The book infation after 2015 requires in depth analysis of the published books.

## **Supervising the next generation academics**
Supervising the next generation of academics is crucial for the continued growth and advancement of academia. As important as the books, book chapters, and articles written by academics are, the theses they supervise are of great importance as students generally tend to copy the practices they have experienced with their advisors. These experiences enable students to pursue careers in academia, perpetuating this cycle throughout their lives. A total of 67 academics (35 professors, 16 associate professors, and 16 faculty members with Ph.D.s) have supervised at least one master's or doctoral thesis to date. Up until the research data was collected, 638 thesis studies (153 doctoral dissertations and 485 master's theses) supervised by academics in our data were conducted. These theses were written by 572 diferent students. Of these students, 94 now work at universities with academic titles. Looking at the distribution of titles, 3 of these students are now professors, 6 are associate professors, 26 are faculty members with Ph.D.s, 16 are research assistants, and 43 are lecturers. Almost all of these 94 academics (91.5%) completed their thesis/dissertations in 2010 or later.
## **Discussion**
The diferences between early-career researchers and more established scholars extend beyond publication and citation metrics to include the networks the latter have built over the years. These networks often provide access to opportunities, collaborations, and resources that are less readily available to ECRs. This disparity highlights the critical role of mentorship and support structures in academia. Advisors and mentors not only ofer guidance but also facilitate connections to broader academic networks, which can signifcantly infuence career trajectories and mitigate some of the challenges faced by ECRs.
The fndings of this study address critical questions about the dynamics within Turkey's associate professorship system, particularly as they afect early-career researchers compared to more established academics. By analyzing the criteria fulfllment and research outputs of various academic ranks, we can discern how well decision-makers meet the expectations set for newer entrants into the academic feld.
#### **Meeting the criteria expected of early‑career researchers**
The fndings of this study reveal signifcant challenges faced by early-career researchers in meeting the criteria expected by the associate professorship system in Turkey. Despite a higher overall publication output among professors, when adjusted for years of experience, there is no signifcant diference in output across academic titles, underscoring the disadvantage faced by ECRs. The data indicates that ECRs exhibit lower publication and citation counts, with the lowest Web of Science publication output and average citation scores observed among faculty members with Ph.D.s, who are at the beginning of their academic careers. The fndings suggest that the h-index may amplify the challenges faced by early-career researchers in felds with low publication and citation densities, such as library and information science. However, it is imperative to acknowledge that this metric ofers a constrained perspective on scholarly contributions and should be interpreted with caution, particularly when assessing researchers at varying stages of their careers. The system's emphasis on international publications, which are often ambiguously defned, disproportionately afects ECRs, who may lack the resources or opportunities to publish in high-impact journals or prestigious international venues. The increase in publications post-2015, driven by academic incentive regulations, underscores systemic issues that prioritize quantity over impact, further complicating the landscape for ECRs striving to meet these evolving expectations.
#### **Comparison of criterion fulfllment between groups**
When comparing criterion fulfllment between decision-makers and early-career researchers, the study identifes stark contrasts. Professors, who often serve as evaluators, display a signifcantly higher publication output, but this advantage diminishes when normalized by years of experience, suggesting that experience plays a crucial role in meeting these criteria. Interestingly, associate professors and faculty members with Ph.D. who have recently obtained associate professorship show the highest citation averages, suggesting that they may be more aligned with current academic expectations. However, the study also uncovers a critical issue: while professors are expected to evaluate ECRs, their own fulfllment of

citation-based criteria is surprisingly low, with the lowest average citation scores among all groups. This discrepancy raises concerns about the fairness and consistency of the evaluation process.
Furthermore, the practice of categorizing Turkish-language articles as international due to system loopholes suggests a conceptual gap that could disproportionately afect ECRs, who may not have the same strategic understanding or opportunities to navigate these ambiguities. The results underscore the need for a more equitable evaluation system that accurately refects the contributions and potential of ECRs, rather than perpetuating systemic advantages held by more experienced academics.
This study is based on quantitative analysis of publication and citation data, which provides valuable insights into patterns and disparities across academic ranks. However, these fndings should be interpreted with caution, as they do not account for qualitative aspects of academic contributions, such as the content, context, or signifcance of individual works. Future research could complement this analysis with textual or qualitative methods to provide a more comprehensive understanding of these dynamics.
Taking these limitations into account, the discussion synthesizes the study's fndings and connects them to the broader context of academic gatekeeping. The analysis highlights the systemic challenges faced by early-career researchers in meeting the associate professorship criteria, particularly the disparities in publication output and citation counts. Additionally, the ambiguity surrounding the defnition of 'international' publications exacerbates these challenges, creating further uncertainty for ECRs. These fndings underscore the need for more equitable evaluation systems that address the structural disadvantages faced by ECRs and provide clearer, fairer criteria for academic progression.
## **Conclusion**
The fndings of this study reveal critical disparities in how the associate professorship criteria impact early-career researchers compared to more established academics. ECRs face signifcant disadvantages due to systemic factors, including lower publication outputs, fewer citations, and challenges arising from the ambiguous defnition of 'international' publications. These disparities highlight the pressing need for a more balanced and equitable evaluation system that better accommodates the diverse contributions of academics at diferent career stages.
This study underscores the importance of critically examining the unintended consequences of the current research evaluation system. Overemphasis on quantitative metrics such as the h-index and publication counts risks encouraging practices like publishing in questionable venues and prioritizing quantity over quality. These challenges not only afect ECRs disproportionately but also have broader implications for academic integrity and innovation.
To address these issues, future reforms should prioritize evaluation frameworks that value diverse research outputs and contributions. This includes developing clearer and more inclusive defnitions for 'international' publications, recognizing collaborative and interdisciplinary work, and incorporating qualitative metrics into the evaluation process. By fostering a more inclusive and supportive academic environment, institutions can mitigate systemic disadvantages and promote equity across career stages.
